superseded_calls.notes: The source Latin phrase "concurrere remote & mediate solum" is rendered as "only remotely and through intermediaries" in English, omitting the explicit "mediate" (i.e., mediated) concurrence. This drops a source clause concerning the manner of divine concurrence, violating completeness.
The English translation accurately renders the Latin source text, preserving all theological nuances regarding secondary causes, immediate and remote causation, without any omissions or additions.

The source Latin states: 'Porro juxta hos Doctores nulla est difficultas in conciliando divino concursu cum libertate actuum humanorum, quandoquidem Deus ad illos immediate non concurrit, sed mediate tantum per liberum arbitrium quod semel creavit & perpetuo conservat.' The English renders this accurately: 'For these teachers, then, reconciling God's concurrence with the freedom of human acts poses no problem at all. God does not act on those acts directly but only through the free choice he created once and keeps in being without interruption.' All seven checks are satisfied: identity, completeness, negation (non concurrit → does not act... directly), agency (Deus... concurrit → God does not act...), modality (no modal shift), doctrine (no theological distortion), scripture (no Scripture citations involved).
The English translation accurately captures the meaning of the Latin text across both paragraphs without dropping clauses or altering agents.

The English adds content not in the Latin source: "a considerable difficulty arises" (from Latin "inde oritur non parva difficultas") is acceptable, but the phrase "how can it be reconciled with the freedom of creatures?" (English para 1) interprets "quomodo illud cum creaturarum libertate constare possit" as a reconciliation question, which is a slight interpretive gloss. More clearly, English para 2 adds "when God moves the will and applies it to its work" twice, which is not verbatim in Latin but reconstructs the logic. However, the core issue is that the English omits the Latin phrase "et rursus quum Deus Voluntatem movet & applicat ad opus" in the second sentence and instead uses "when God moves the will and applies it to its work" as a reconstructive phrase, which, while semantically close, is not a direct rendering and introduces slight rephrasing that alters the original syntactic structure. This constitutes a failure of strict completeness under the requirement that no source clause be dropped or invented, even if meaning is preserved. The English does not render the Latin clause "et rursus quum Deus Voluntatem movet & applicat ad opus" as a direct clause but rephrases it, thus failing literal clause preservation.
The English translation accurately and completely captures the entire Latin source paragraph without omitting clauses, altering agencies, or distorting theological terminology.

Source paragraph 1 mentions 'necessariam esse ad agendum praeviam quandam Dei motionem & applicationem' and 'Statuunt enim Deum, absque ulla consideratione istiusmodi negativae determinationis quae in Voluntate creata praecesserit, Voluntatem pro suo arbitrio movere; neque movere simpliciter, sed ad sic, vel sic operandum efficaciter impellere' but English paragraph 2 omits the nuance that God moves the will 'pro suo arbitrio' (according to His own will/choice) and instead says 'as he chooses' which is acceptable, yet the omission of 'pro suo arbitrio' as a distinct theological qualification and the simplification of 'neque movere simpliciter, sed ad sic, vel sic operandum efficaciter impellere' to 'He does not merely move it but effectively drives it to act in this way or that' loses the precise contrast between simple motion and efficacious impulsion to act in a specific way. This constitutes a dropped clause in the sense of semantic weakening, violating completeness.

The English translation accurately and completely reflects the Latin text, preserving theological terminology, agency, and modal structures across its two paragraphs without any omissions or additions.

English paragraph 1 drops the Latin clause 'in Summa Operis de Auxiliis divinae gratiae libro secundo' and instead renders it as 'in the summary of his work on the helps of divine grace, book 2', which omits the specific title 'Summa Operis' and alters the structure; this constitutes a dropped source clause and invented phrasing not present in the Latin.

The translation accurately and clearly renders the Latin source text without any omissions, additions, or doctrinal distortions, correctly capturing all agents, modalities, and philosophical-theological terminology such as physical cause and predetermination.
